items.title: The former weakness key to Red Bull's sudden supremacy
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
While Mercedes’ troubled upgrade removed it as a factor, Red Bull’s rivals see signs in its maiden pole position as an engine manufacturer of a proper shuffle in Formula 1's competitive order.

Max Verstappen’s first pole since last year’s title-deciding Abu Dhabi Grand Prix certainly owed nothing to good fortune. He was quickest in all three qualifying segments. Proof of the RB22’s pace was made firm with Isack Hadjar ending up third on the timesheets.

But it is not the Red Bull result that has surprised the opposition. Instead, it is how it was achieved.

A deep dive into the telemetry data of where the pace has come from suggests a reset in the performance profile of the top squads – with areas where teams had previously been strong no longer true this weekend.

As detailed below, on the Sepang straights Verstappen was super strong, while in the high-speed and medium-speed corners where Red Bull was being murdered by the other frontrunners earlier in the year, it was now right up there.

This points to Red Bull having addressed the key weaknesses that had held it back.

It has got more out of its all-new 2026 power units and, rivals suspect, its Baku upgrade unleashed far more potential from the car in areas where it was lagging that had been on show in Azerbaijan.

There is no single magic bullet in F1 that ever leapfrogs a team forward, and observing Red Bull’s form over the season points to it having just steadily chipped away.

Miami and Austria upgrades addressed some of its high- and medium-speed corner deficit. So, with more getting unleashed from better energy management too, by Madrid – a track with a good mixture of high, medium and low speed corners, it was within touching distance of pole as Verstappen missed out there by 0.140 seconds.

Its Baku upgrade had not shown itself to be a game-changing last weekend, especially with Verstappen having been slowed by power unit problems.

But the layout of the circuit there is all about low speed and straights – and the pace on Sunday showed how close it was.

So it was only in Malaysia, where there is a much better combination of high- and medium-speed corners, that the true potential of that upgrade has perhaps emerged.

McLaren boss Andrea Stella certainly thinks that there has been a change of trend here, which he hints may have come from a "significant step" Red Bull’s Baku upgrade gave it.

Asked by The Race about whether he had seen a change in the performance profile of the top squads, he said: “It's interesting here in Malaysia to see that the straightline speed advantage that Mercedes had in Baku, we don't see it. It's kind of disappeared.

“The best performance in a straightline seems to be, by a decent margin, Red Bull. The best cornering performance is Ferrari. And we, McLaren…are also puzzled a little bit by the fact that in high speed, we are no longer the best car, like we seemed to be in Madrid, or we seemed to be in Zandvoort.”

Verstappen himself concurred that Red Bull’s recent upgrades had “pushed some of the weaknesses out of the car” as he suggested this result was simply down to the team having understood its car a lot better.

With increased downforce comes more grip and a better balance – and a virtuous circle with the gains that then come from the tyres.

Plus, added Verstappen: “on a track probably where it’s all very hot and you want a stable balance or connected balance, then that’s very important. And that’s, I think, what we have found a little bit more over the last weekends".

It was interesting to hear Hadjar talk about how, when he returned to the car in Baku, it felt different to when he had last raced before the summer break.

“I definitely feel like I jumped in a car that’s way better than when I left it in Budapest,” he said. “Definitely, when you step out actually for three races and you come back, you actually notice a bigger difference.”

Yet despite what everyone has seen of Red Bull this weekend, there remain a few caveats before suggesting this is the start of a new chapter in the F1 2026 season.

Mercedes falling back may be a one-off, plus Malaysia’s heat and rough surface make it an outlier – both in terms of tyre management and set-up and aero characteristics that include cooling compromises.

So the proof of where things stand up may have to wait until Singapore next weekend.

How Verstappen beat Hamilton to pole

What really stood out about Verstappen’s pole position lap was the level of confidence visible from the onboard footage. I can’t remember an occasion in 2026 when he’s looked so at one with the car, so it was no surprise that he referred to its “connected balance”.

He could brake late, turn in decisively, and on the few occasions when the car required any corrective action, he was able to do it quickly and with the minimum of fuss. 

That said, it wasn’t in the corners that Verstappen built his decisive advantage. There, it was about getting the most out of a package that is significantly improved but still usually not market-leading in turns. Where he could make hay was on the straights and in the braking zones.

Although Verstappen’s pole position margin was three-tenths of a second over Hamilton, the battle for pole position only swung decisively in his favour in the final sector. There, he was a mighty 0.464s quicker than closest rival Lewis Hamilton.

The strong straightline speed of the RB22 showed immediately at the start of the lap, gaining around a tenth over Hamilton (with a similar margin over the McLaren of Lando Norris and Kimi Antonelli’s Mercedes) by the first corner based on when all were at 100% throttle. Relative to Hamilton, he emerged from Turn 2 with a similar advantage and by the end of the first sector, 145 metres before Turn 4, he had a 0.138s edge over Hamilton - and just over three-tenths over both Antonelli and Norris.

Sector 2 was the weak point for the Red Bull, the fast, flowing section bookended by slow corners where the battle swung towards Hamilton - who generally registered a similar or higher minimum speed in this section and took 0.304s out of Verstappen - putting him 0.166s up entering the final sector. 

Much of the final sector is at full throttle, and it was here that Verstappen demolished Hamilton by 0.464s on his pole lap - although it should be noted that Leclerc was actually the faster Ferrari driver through here with a deficit to the Red Bull of only 0.2s. 

Although Hamilton was a little quicker in the Turn 11 right-hander than Verstappen, this sector was mainly Red Bull territory.

This all added up to an emphatic pole position after a performance that was all about Verstappen being at his brilliant best in the corners in an improved car that gave him the balance he needed and cashing in on the straights.

items.title: McLaren puzzled by persistent Norris-only F1 car problem
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Lando Norris has a straightline speed deficit to team-mate Oscar Piastri for the second Formula 1 weekend running in Malaysia, one his McLaren team doesn’t understand. 

Norris struggled with a small straightline deficit on his McLaren in Baku versus Piastri, because of an issue that the team suspected was linked to fuel injection in the power unit. 

That deficit is still present at Sepang where Norris was over six tenths off pole in qualifying sixth, albeit 0.005s ahead of Piastri. 

"I felt like my lap was very strong…I'm still struggling a lot in the straights everywhere. I'm just down on every single straight," Norris said. 

"Every time I get a good exit, I'm just slower in the end of the straight. It just hurts seeing this every single time, so I should be higher up, not because I could have done a better job necessarily, but just because we're not getting everything out of the car that we need to. 

"That doesn't [just] make my life tough today, but it also makes it tough for tomorrow."

The straightline speed deficit between Norris (white line) and Piastri (orange line) in qualifying is clear when you look at the data for the second half of their fastest Q3 laps. 

"We should say that the issue we see on Lando’s car is about a lack of straightline speed," McLaren team boss Andrea Stella confirmed after qualifying. 

"So we see that in the power limited section, the car accelerates a little less and develops a little bit less top speed, all the other parameters being the same. We talk about probably between one and two kph, like they are small quantities. 

"They are even difficult to see because as soon as Lando, for instance, has a little bit of slipstream from a car four seconds ahead, now you see Lando faster than the other car. 

"It’s small quantities that we see statistically and we should more precisely talk about the deficit of straightline speed. OK, which we can quantify in a laptime loss that I would say in excess of one tenth of a second, possibly between one and two tenths of a second."

McLaren doesn’t understand what’s behind the issue and it won’t be able to fix it until the next race in Singapore at the earliest, meaning Norris will have to suffer with it through this grand prix. 

"[It’s a] different conversation is about why that is and why we can talk immediately about a lack of power," Stella added.

"In reality, there can be different reasons. It's more difficult to monitor what is happening from a power unit point of view because if it was deployment, we would be able to see it possibly has to do with some other parameters.

"But at the same time, there's behaviours of the power unit that depend on what's happening on the chassis side. 

"Finally, there could be parameters that have to do with the drag of the car.

"So it's at no point we are making a point about power unit. We are just making a point about a lack of straightline speed, which we want to make a point about because it's fair to Lando that we take the responsibility for the fact that on his car, there's a laptime deficit, which at the moment we have not been able to remove in a couple of events.

"But obviously, we are definitely looking at all the possible parameters, and we will look at further changes, but we only can do that now for Singapore."

items.title: Mercedes' upgrade letdown - What we know
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Mercedes is scrambling to understand why its upgrade appears to have taken it backwards rather than forwards at Formula 1’s Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Dominant 2026 championship leader Mercedes suffered its "toughest Saturday" of the season at Sepang, with Kimi Antonelli and George Russell fourth and eighth, half a second adrift of Max Verstappen’s polesitting Red Bull.

That’s despite Mercedes introducing a major car upgrade that pre-event simulations predicted would bring a laptime improvement of around three tenths.

“You're expecting 0.3s gain to kick in and it looks like 0.3s or 0.4s or 0.5s backwards,” Toto Wolff told Sky Sports F1.

“[It’s the] first time we miss out on the top three and by quite a chunk, so... Odd. But I guess we will find a solution.”

Mercedes was outside the top three in qualifying in Hungary too, but with a deficit that’s almost half of what it faces at Sepang.

So what’s going on? Has the upgrade not delivered as expected, how much is down to the unique characteristics of Sepang and can Mercedes hope for better in the grand prix?

Mercedes wasn’t helped by having its toughest Friday of the season so far, as weaknesses that it hasn’t suffered with all year appeared.

“We have been a little bit caught out on Friday with some car behaviour that we didn't see all year,” Wolff explained.

“But it's very hot and the tarmac is very different to all the tracks. It looked really good in [FP3] we seem to have, at least with Kimi , made a step in understanding. Then qualifying was a little bit back to what we saw before, just no performance.”

Asked what that unwanted car behaviour was, Wolff said: “It looks like we are very draggy, because it's the first time that we're losing a lot of time on the straights to especially Max [Verstappen].

“Then through the low speed, Turn 2 we are not able to turn the car. There's just too much understeer. So overall things we haven't seen all year.”

The data backs that up with Antonelli losing three of the five tenths to Verstappen through the low-speed Turns 1-2 alone in Q3.

Mercedes can’t rely on its usual straightline advantage on the back straight and the start/finish straight as Verstappen (blue) gains another two tenths on Antonelli (green) from the run out of the Turn 14 right-hander to the line.

“With this new package, obviously the window of the way the car operates is different,” Antonelli said.

“We're trying to understand in which window the car performance is best. In the high-speed, our performance has been very strong this weekend, but in the low-speed is where we lacked.

“Overall we need to understand why and try to move on and improve.”

Is the upgrade actually working?

So is the Mercedes upgrade working as expected but being blighted by Sepang’s unique conditions (the aged tarmac, the long radius low-speed corners), or is the upgrade mis-firing versus expectations?

“Well, that is the big question mark,” Russell said when that was put to him.

“If you could have done a direct back-to-back, it would have been great to know, but that's the challenge of this sport.

“If I put the upgrade package on last week [in Baku], even if it was worse, we probably still would have been on pole and we'd have been saying it was fantastic.

“Equally, if we had the old car here, maybe the result would have been even worse. So that's the challenge.

“As a team, we have yet to have a bad race this whole season and this was clearly a very bad qualifying for us.”

Russell had taken pole position by over eight tenths in Baku, the biggest pole margin of the season, but the team always expected Sepang to be tougher because it’s a less favourable circuit for its car.

“The whole year whenever we went on tracks like this with very open tarmac, we've always struggled,” Antonelli said.

“So is it because of the tarmac and because it's so hot out there? Or is it because maybe we're missing something with the new package? So it's really hard to understand.

“But we try to do our best and probably Singapore will give us a better read on the package.”

Russell described the track surface as “like driving on gravel” and that’s clearly hurting Mercedes more than other teams.

There is an element of qualifying looking worse on paper because Antonelli wasted a set of tyres after a Q2 track limits deletion, which prompted him to run earlier than others in Q3 on a single set of tyres.

“I understeered off the track, but I think with a clean qualifying, probably P2, maybe P3 on the road, but not P1,” Antonelli said. “Max was a bit too quick for us today.”

But there is still undoubtedly a sense of disappointment at Mercedes about how the upgrade debut has gone with Russell calling it the “toughest Saturday of the year” so far.

“All the numbers say it's an improvement, but obviously it's a sport that we need to follow the laptimes and not what the numbers say,” Russell said.

“So the numbers look absolutely fine and in line with expectations, but the result wasn't.”

Ultimately there isn’t one reason for Mercedes’ struggles, as Wolff said: “There are many factors we will need to take into consideration, and we can’t rule anything out at this stage”.

There's only so much Mercedes can do more before the grand prix though with only minor set-up tweaks allowed under the parc ferme rules.

"I think we have a good opportunity tomorrow starting on the clean side," Antonelli said, and he'll be third because of Isack Hadjar's grid penalty for taking a seventh engine of the year.

"But I still believe that Red Bull still has the upper edge on pace and Ferrari is very close. But we'll do our best. I think track position is going to be very important.

"We'll try to manage those tyres the best way as possible. And then try to, if we can fight for the win, great. If we have to settle for P2 or P3, we'll take that."

The real challenge for Mercedes will come in the coming days as it bids to understand exactly why it's seemingly gone backwards.

And it will need to optimise this new package as rolling back to a previous spec car isn’t really an option, given the older spec parts were very near the end of their life, and producing new versions would take an unplanned bite out of its strict cost cap allowance.

items.title: Winners and losers from shock Malaysia F1 qualifying
items.author: The Race Team
items.content:
Red Bull catapulting to the top of the order for its first pole of the year, the first for a non-Mercedes powered car in 2026, grabbed the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia headlines.

And that makes our winners and losers feature even more of a goldmine, as we assess the best and worst performances of the day.

Loser: Mercedes (4th & 8th)

This was Mercedes’ worst qualifying performance since Hungary, where Kimi Antonelli was fourth and George Russell seventh, and the temptation is to conclude the substantial upgrade Mercedes brought to Malaysia isn’t working.

Team boss Toto Wolff told Sky Sports F1 that Mercedes "still believe the upgrade works" but will need to comb through the data after discovering the car "looks like we are very draggy".

"It’s the first time that we're losing a lot of time on the straights, to especially Max," Wolff added. “And then through the low speed, Turn 2, we are not able to turn the car. There's just too much understeer. So overall things we haven't seen all year."

Both Russell and Antonelli pointed to the "abrasiveness of the tarmac" (Russell’s words) making Sepang an outlier circuit, with Antonelli suggesting "the whole year, whenever we went on tracks like this with very open tarmac, we've always struggled.

"So is it because of the tarmac and because it's so hot out there? Or is it because maybe we're missing something with the new package?"

Mercedes is a bit stuck right now, because it definitely feels the upgrade has improved the car in high-speed corners, as it was designed to do, but that seems to have come at the cost of its previous strengths through low-speed corners and in straight-line efficiency.

And now the cars are in parc ferme after qualifying, there’s no going back unless you want to start from the pitlane, and in any case the old parts were reaching the end of their natural life, so under the cost cap Mercedes can't afford to revert and needs to find a way to make this work.

"All the numbers say it's an improvement," said Russell. "But obviously it's a sport that we need to follow the laptimes and not what the numbers say.

"The numbers look absolutely fine and in line with expectations, but the result wasn’t."

Winner: Max Verstappen (1st)

Nine years on, Max Verstappen and Red Bull are still the quickest combination around Sepang and who’d bet against him in the race?

Having not been on pole position all season, Verstappen looked relatively comfortable throughout qualifying, topping each session and taking pole with a three-tenth margin.

Team-mate Isack Hadjar completed a strong day for Red Bull (even if he’ll go back five places on the grid), but Verstappen’s four-tenth margin over him shows the difference the four-time world champion made.

Winner: Aston Martin (12th & 14th)

Easily Aston Martin-Honda’s best performance of the season so far, combining the lighter B-spec car first introduced in Hungary with Honda’s ADUO 2 upgraded engine - which doesn’t seem to be a giant leap but is at least not penalising the car to quite the extent Honda’s engine has been doing so far in 2026.

Alonso was just over four tenths away from making Q3, while Lance Stroll - who felt the car "clicked for me during the second push lap in Q1 and came together much better" - was only two places and 0.346s further back, and might have done better but for some scruffy driving in Q2.

In a piece of signature Alonso hyperbole, he called it a "miracle that we are fighting with cars that are much faster than us".

"No doubts our best weekend in terms of car performance," and "definitely a step forward in terms of competitiveness," Alonso also said.

"The car is exactly the same as the last four rounds, since Budapest, so it’s just telling us that it depends on the circuit layout and the amount of straights we have, we can be more or less competitive."

Although it should be said he expects to go backwards not forwards on Sunday, owing to the aforementioned "miracle" and "some fast cars starting behind us with some penalties as well that tomorrow they will come strong".

Winner: Lewis Hamilton (2nd)

Ferrari’s qualifying execution has been a consistent bugbear for Lewis Hamilton for much of his time at the team, but Hamilton called Ferrari's Malaysia timing "perfect".

He said he was surprised to be on the front row for the first time since Barcelona, having been looking at the third row pre-qualifying.

"These cars are so sensitive; you make the smallest change and it’s ridiculous the difference it can make from one run, one session to the other," Hamilton said.

"One click of front wing or one millimetre ride height, a quarter degree of camber, 0.1 of toe, something like that. These little things make such a big difference to balance, it’s literally a moving target that you’re trying to work around, with set-up and also the controls we have.

"Even understanding throttle application, if you get to full throttle too early here, your stair [ramp down] starts early and you lose time down the straights. These things that I don’t think many of us like.

"Mastering all of that together is a massive challenge. We’re so on the edge because we’re losing so much on the straights."

Winner: Gabriel Bortoleto (10th)

His Audi team-mate went out in Q1 and he made it all the way through to Q3, so Gabriel Bortoleto can sleep well knowing he had a good day.

The Audi squad looked like it went backwards in Baku, despite its massive upgrade package, but thanks to soul-searching and "long nights" at the factory, it appears to be unlocking some of that new performance.

That, plus what Bortoleto described as "when you do very good laps and the car is in a good window and you feel comfortable, you can sometimes do something great".

Self-proclaimed "greatness" can be jarring, but its hard to deny Bortoleto a dose of that today.

Winner: Valtteri Bottas (21st)

Valtteri Bottas looked "pretty slow" in Baku by his own admission, so qualifying over three tenths ahead of Cadillac team-mate Sergio Perez in Malaysia was the perfect response.

He has the upgraded Ferrari ADUO 2 engine for the first time this weekend, something Perez elected not to run, having used it in Baku, to save the mileage on it for a different track.

"There is a difference. It's not huge difference, but there is a difference, so it's nice to have it," Bottas said of the engine upgrade.

Asked by The Race if he felt like he was back on form after Baku, Bottas said: "Something was definitely off last weekend, we were so far off, but we changed many things and now the car is again back to normal.

"No issues at all this weekend, so being able to just get to the rhythm, do the set-up work and go from there."

Two races with Williams' new upgrade, twice beaten by his team-mate. This wasn't a good day for Alex Albon.

While Carlos Sainz said he did better laps than the Baku ones that got him into Q3 and perhaps his best this year, Albon was another victim of running wide at the Turn 14 right-hander that leads onto the back straight.

But Albon reckons the team has been "struggling with parts" - quality rather than quantity in this case - and a change for qualifying "made it worse". So perhaps that explains the deficit between the pair.

"If we need to do a pitlane start tomorrow [to change the parts], so be it," he added.

Loser: Haas (18th and 19th)

The worst qualifying result of Haas’s 2026 F1 season comes right off the back of the team’s first double points finish of the year.

Esteban Ocon felt he was sent out too early in Q1, so he missed the best of the track conditions, while Ollie Bearman says he was compromised by messy practice sessions, including the wrong set-up being applied to his car.

"For me, the issue has been an all-weekend long one," Bearman said. “We started out in FP1, it was okay, but then in FP2 we had a problem with the car set-up.

"Basically, the set-up that we intended to put on the car was not the set-up that ended up on the car.

"The car ended up in a state that we would never intend to ever run a race car, not even on an oval.

"The only time I've actually had a good car and had a good feeling was in that final [qualifying] run.

"I didn't get everything out of the tyre because it was the first time I had a decent balance all weekend."

Loser: Nico Hulkenberg (17th)

A big moment at Turn 14 undid Nico Hulkenberg's chances of going any further by 0.087s, out in Q1.

That might have been dismissed as normal looking at the team's performance in Baku, but we already know Bortoleto put the car in Q3, so this can only go down as an error that creates an embarrassing qualifying deficit to the only person you can compare Hulkenberg to, his team-mate.

"Disappointed with myself, didn't put the lap together," was his take.

Hulkenberg has a wily way of overturning these set-backs on race day, so don't count him out.

Especially as Bortoleto has proven Audi's lack of straight-line speed - which won't improve much for the remainder of the season - won't be the thing that holds Audi back from fighting through the midfield this weekend.

items.title: Winners and losers from MotoGP's Motegi sprint
items.author: Eden Hannigan
items.content:
Marc Marquez produced a dominant Motegi sprint victory to cut into Jorge Martin’s advantage at the top of the MotoGP riders’ standings to just seven points.

After a first-lap pile-up, some surprise podium contenders and two important post-race penalties, here are our winners and losers from the 12-lap sprint.

Winner: Marc Marquez (1st) 

Another sprint win and more points gained in the increasingly yo-yoing championship battle was pretty much the maximum Marquez could take from Saturday. 

After he missed out on pole to Martin, it was pretty clear another “Marquez strategy” would be deployed - start fast, get the lead at the first corner and not look back, as he’d done in Aragon and Misano. Leaving Martin out to dry on the exit of Turn 1 in what was basically a copy-and-paste from those two races, he marched to victory.

He was also very gracious to “one of the most talented riders” he’s ever seen in Diogo Moreira for taking an extra two points away from title rival Martin. After all, every little bit helps.

Loser: Alex Marquez (DNF)

It’s hard to understand quite what Alex Marquez thought he was going to do when he went steaming into Turn 3, got it all wrong under braking and acted as a bowling ball with an unfortunate Pedro Acosta and Fabio Di Giannantonio the pins. 

Marquez didn’t do a post-race debrief to explain his side. Instead, he sent a brief voice note via Gresini - saying he felt "so, so sorry” for ruining the race of two riders, as well as his own.

Just not a good move, which has rightly been punished.

Winner: Diogo Moreira (2nd)

Moreira described his podium repeatedly as "not a real result", seemingly to keep expectations in check for Sunday - but, though the Alex Marquez-initiated attrition certainly played a big role, it wasn't at all surprising Moreira was one to benefit.

Maybe not faster at Motegi than team-mate Johann Zarco, but seemingly less on edge, he looked a seasoned veteran navigating his way past Marco Bezzecchi and Ai Ogura - and kept his cool on the final lap exiting Turn 10 while the two riders ahead tripped up with track limits.

Among the better rides of a really strong rookie season - and please, Honda, announce his 2027 seat already.

Loser: Jorge Martin (3rd)

Martin was surprisingly calm about the post-race penalty that cost him second place and two points versus Marquez in the title fight, describing it as a “pity” rather than a big deal. 

Part of that calmness might come from an understanding it could have been worse. Facing tyre problems that forced him into management from mid-race distance, Martin “couldn’t do anything, was just spinning til sixth gear” in the final stages of a sprint he was ultimately relieved to finish.

The Aprilia rider stressed it wasn’t an issue of conventional tyre wear but rather overheating at the centre. He was running out of options there - and minus a rear wing, as he was chased down by Moreira and Enea Bastianini on the final lap. 

Martin was happy with a podium and his overall pace, but some alarm bells may be ringing ahead of the grand prix.

Loser: Marco Bezzecchi (6th)

The three-bike crash and Martin's track limits slip-up mitigated what could have been a bad championship day for Bezzecchi into just a bad one.

Slightly underwhelmed by his performance on the soft rear on Friday, he was tempted by the medium rear after strong pace in morning practice - but it never translated at all in the race.

His pace held up, and unlike for other medium-tyre runner Jack Miller there was no blistering - but the peak pace was super-weak, so he got muscled down the order. Martin's example showed the soft rear was precarious - but also that it was the right choice.

Honda is best-positioned of any MotoGP manufacturer, obviously, to adjust to any changes to Motegi (a circuit it owns), so it isn't too surprising to see a result like this out of step with the RC213V's recent form.

Still, it's very welcome. Honda has been spinning the wheels on its season - Joan Mir sidelined, Luca Marini still struggling to qualify, upgrades non-existent while work is full steam ahead on the 850cc bike - but Moreira's big performance keeps the ennui at bay.

The extremely capable stand-in efforts by Somkiat Chantra, too, show that the bike is genuinely delivering the goods.

Also doesn't hurt that Honda's big rider signing for 2027 - more on him later - had another very strong day.

Loser: Pecco Bagnaia (DNF)

Bagnaia shredding the centre of his rear tyre has already had consequences on the wider weekend - with Michelin removing its soft rear tyre from its allocation for the race - but for him it cost a point at best, as he was too limited by grid position anyway.

He might be totally faultless in the state of the tyre, but for the last year and a half it feels like he has a worse relationship with the rear Michelin than anyone else within the Ducati camp - so his season-long rear grip struggle probably exacerbated the issue here.

Winner: Enea Bastianini (4th)

No podium due to track limits - and an instant-classic VAR gesture at the finish to show his discontent.

But it's easy to let go of the disappointment given Bastianini has looked the most lively he has in many rounds, as he serves out his Tech3 KTM 'notice period' before pivoting to Trackhouse Aprilia.

"It has been different and it's very beautiful to be again on top, fighting for something good," he rejoiced - and a long-awaited good qualifying was central to this.

Winner: Fabio Quartararo (9th)

The Honda-bound Quartararo has been in a really good groove since his extinguished fallout with Yamaha at Aragon - and the trend has continued here.

Though his edge over the other Yamahas appears slightly flattered by a very strange day for Jack Miller, who is probably closest on underlying pace, it remains the case that only Quartararo could drag the M1 anywhere near the points here.

Attrition obviously helped, but it still took an above-expectations effort to keep the Ducati of Fermin Aldeguer behind.

Loser: Brad Binder (18th)

“A Saturday to forget” was how Binder summed up his day, and it’s hard to disagree with his assessment as he finished 18th and last of the sprint runners.

Binder’s issues were compounded by feeling like he’d “been driven over like a friggin' bus” after a qualifying crash - which saw the mechanics across both KTM garages and Tech3 assemble to get his bike ready in time for the sprint.

From there on, it also wasn’t great - with issues at Turn 1 culminating in him riding straight across the gravel due to chatter and locking.

items.title: Michelin makes major Motegi tyre decision after sprint dramas
items.author: Simon Patterson
items.content:
Michelin will remove its softest rear compound from the allocation for Sunday’s Japanese Grand Prix following multiple instances of tyres blistering during Saturday’s half-distance sprint race at Motegi.

But it will not, despite lobbying from some teams, make its emergency hard-construction tyre mandatory for the race.

It became apparent during the latter stages of the sprint at Motegi that numerous riders were struggling with their rear tyres delaminating, something that was predicted as a possible concern on the newly-resurfaced Motegi asphalt.

Pecco Bagnaia was forced to retire from the race with one lap to go, while championship leader Jorge Martin was lucky to hold on to a podium place, finishing the race missing pieces of the rear aerodynamics of his Aprilia after they were shattered by his disintegrating rear tyre.

That delamination, a symptom of low wear and high grip that causes a build-up of excess temperatures, was something that Michelin had predicted might be an issue - with the French firm coming prepared with a third rear option using the special construction designed to cope with the high heat that similar tracks like the Red Bull Ring force onto the tyre.

“With the new asphalt we never tested here,” Michelin boss Piero Taramasso exclusively told The Race after the sprint. “We know Motegi is a demanding track, and that is why we decided to bring a third rear specification.

“In the meeting on Thursday, we already spoke with the riders and the teams, and told them to be careful and to check the temperature of the tyres. It [the soft rear] was at the limit, yesterday and this morning, almost for everyone, but we said 'OK, for 12 laps, we can try it.'

“After the sprint, there were three bikes with quite bad blisters. The blistering is when you generate a lot of heat inside the compound. The construction stays intact, but you get bubbles inside the compound and it opens up and makes holes.”

It’s believed by The Race’s sources in the paddock that a number of teams subsequently called for Michelin to make the aforementioned hard tyre, brought specifically for this situation, mandatory for Sunday’s race.

But these teams have not managed to persuade Michelin to take that step - given that, according to Taramasso, a number of rivals had no issues on Saturday.

“We know that in the sprints,” he told The Race, “the riders don’t manage anything, they just go full, so probably the situation tomorrow will be a bit better.

“We spoke with Dorna, and the decision for the race is that the rear soft won’t be allowed, and they will have to work with the medium or the hard one. The Michelin suggestion, we really strongly suggest to use the rear hard. That’s why we brought it here, but now it’s up to the teams and the riders to decide.

“There are some bikes, like the KTMs, some Hondas, that don’t have the problem. They manage well to not put a lot of energy in the tyres, and we don’t want to penalise them and oblige everyone to go with the hard, even if we suggest it very strongly.”

That is likely going to leave a number of teams in something of a dilemma for the main race, though, given that Jack Miller - one of only two riders alongside Marco Bezzecchi to use the medium in the sprint - also experienced similar blistering issues.

“We had two mediums on track,” Taramasso added, “and Marco was clean but Jack had some blistering, too. The medium is stronger compared to the soft, but if your bike’s setting is not optimum and you have some more spin, then what you have to do is do everything in your power to limit the spin and put less energy into the rear tyre.”

The decision not to make the hard tyre mandatory will come as welcome relief to some, most notably sprint race winner Marc Marquez, whose factory Ducati has struggled all season to use the heat-resistant rear construction, conceding valuable championship points last time out at Austria to the factory Aprilia duo of Martin and Bezzecchi.

Given the hard option has been roundly ignored by teams so far in practice this weekend, Sunday's warm-up has been extended from the customary 10 minutes to 20 at Michelin's request, "in order to allow all riders to evaluate" the hard tyre.

items.title: Verstappen takes first Red Bull F1 pole of 2026
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Max Verstappen claimed the first non-Mercedes-powered pole position of the 2026 Formula 1 season so far, while Mercedes suffered its worst qualifying of the year despite debuting upgrades at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Verstappen topped Q1, Q2 and Q3 at Sepang en route to his first pole position since the 2025 Abu Dhabi title-decider, beating his former title rival Lewis Hamilton by three tenths.

Hamilton praised the “perfect timing” of his qualifying run as he claimed his first front row since June's Barcelona Grand Prix, which he won.

Isack Hadjar made it two Red Bulls in the top three as the team followed up its strong Baku weekend.

But Hadjar won’t start third as he has a five-place grid penalty for taking a seventh internal combustion engine of the season.

Kimi Antonelli qualified fourth in the upgraded Mercedes, half a second down on poleman Verstappen running off sync with an earlier final lap after a Q2 track limits penalty set him back and cost a set of tyres, while team-mate George Russell was down in eighth.

That’s the weakest qualifying result of Mercedes’ 2026 season so far, eclipsing the fourth and seventh in Hungary in July.

Charles Leclerc was fifth ahead of McLaren duo Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri.

The top 10 was rounded out by Russell, Pierre Gasly’s Alpine and Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto.

'Miracle' double Q2 for Aston Martin

Arvid Lindblad, carrying a back-of-the-grid penalty for taking new engine components this weekend, sacrificed his Q2 to try tow team-mate Liam Lawson into Q3.

Lindblad gave Lawson a strong tow on the back straight, but Lawson still ended up two tenths shy of a place in Q3 in 11th.

Fernando Alonso was a season’s best 12th for Aston Martin, declaring it a “miracle” afterwards as it’s only his second Q2 appearance of the year.

And for the first time this year team-mate Lance Stroll made it through to Q2, lapping only 0.008s slower than Alonso in Q1, before ending up three tenths off Alonso in Q2 in 14th.

Carlos Sainz’s Williams split the Aston Martins in 13th place while Franco Colapinto was 15th, having not set a time in Q2 either because of his 15-place grid penalty - five for causing the Baku pile-up and 10 for fresh engine components.

Nico Hulkenberg and Alex Albon both made costly errors at the penultimate corner, compromising their final laps and leaving them eliminated in Q1 in 17th and 20th.

Haas suffered its first double Q1 exit since Monaco with Ollie Bearman and Esteban Ocon 18th and 19th.

Ocon was the first driver to take the chequered flag and told his team “I think we went too early” after his elimination.

Valtteri Bottas continued his bounceback from a miserable Azerbaijan Grand Prix, qualifying over three tenths quicker than Cadillac team-mate Sergio Perez - the first time he’s outqualified a team-mate at Sepang in six attempts.

items.title: Alex Marquez gets hefty penalty for multi-bike Motegi crash
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
Gresini Ducati rider Alex Marquez will serve a double long-lap penalty in Sunday's Japanese Grand Prix at Motegi for causing a multi-bike crash in the sprint.

Marquez was attacking fellow Ducati rider Fabio Di Giannantonio for sixth place coming into Turn 3 on the opening lap, but ran out of room to navigate the corner as Pedro Acosta cut back in after being forced to the outside by Bastianini.

Marquez thus lost the front in trying desperately to slow down, hitting Acosta, before his bike then also collected Di Giannantonio on the outside.

He will retain fifth on the grid on Sunday but will be compromised by a double long-lap assessed by the Simon Crafar-led stewards' panel, despite this being a first offence this season for the Gresini man.

Incidentally, the crash eliminated Marquez's future KTM team-mate in Di Giannantonio and his future employer's lead rider in Acosta.

Other double long-lap penalties this season included one for Joan Mir for ignoring a black-and-orange flag and ones for Jorge Martin and Johann Zarco for causing multi-rider pile-ups at the start.

Speaking to media after the sprint, Acosta said that incidents like these happened in racing but semi-chastised Marquez for "trying to get a podium quite early".

He also lamented a lost opportunity to make up points on third-placed-in-the-standings Marco Bezzecchi, believing that a podium - though likely not a win - was on the cards had he stayed on.

Marquez, meanwhile, said he accepted the penalty and that he had made a mistake, and apologised for ending his rivals' races.

items.title: Marquez beats penalised Martin in Motegi sprint, Moreira stars
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
Ducati MotoGP rider Marc Marquez took five points out of a penalised Jorge Martin's championship lead with a commanding win in the Motegi sprint.

Marquez picked off Martin at the start, setting up the move through Turn 1 and completing it through Turn 2.

No real victory battle materialised from there as Marquez established a one-second buffer and managed it from there on out, with Martin looking to settle what should have been - but wasn't - an equally-comfortable second place.

Both anyway gained significant ground on outside title hopeful Marco Bezzecchi, who had a very poor race despite being aided by attrition.

Three rivals were removed from the podium battle as, after being overtaken into Turn 3 by Enea Bastianini, Pedro Acosta cut back in to take the corner and was then wiped out by a too-fast Alex Marquez, with Fabio Di Giannantonio also taken down.

But Bezzecchi was one of two riders to have selected the medium rear for the race in lieu of the soft, and the choice proved downright disastrous.Third after the start, he had no pace to stay with the leading duo and was swallowed up by Bastianini, as well as Diogo Moreira and Ai Ogura.

Moreira had overtaken Ogura while the latter was trying to make his way past Bezzecchi, and then set off after a podium. He reeled in Bastianini towards the end, and both suddenly closed in massively on Martin.

Neither made the move, but both Martin and Bastianini fell foul of track limits on the final lap, catching the green paint coming off the kerb at Turn 10 - and thus promoting Moreira to a remarkable second place.

The penalties meant Martin is now only seven points ahead of Marquez, with Bezzecchi 45 down on his team-mate.

Ogura took fifth place ahead of Bezzecchi, followed by Johann Zarco and Raul Fernandez - who had engaged in a back-and-forth duel through the race.

Fabio Quartararo snuck into ninth, fending off Fermin Aldeguer late on and ensuring that all five manufacturers scored in the sprint.

The only rider to retire besides the three involved in the opening-lap crash was Pecco Bagnaia, last year's grand prix-and-sprint winner, who ran 13th but came in on the final lap with a shredded rear tyre.

items.title: What went on in final Sepang F1 practice
items.author: Ben Anderson
items.content:
Formula 1 championship leader Kimi Antonelli set the pace in final practice for F1’s Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, as Mercedes recovered from its most difficult Friday of 2026 to lead the way with its heavily upgraded car.

Deputy team principal Bradley Lord said Mercedes conducted overnight simulator work to figure out why the upgrades had improved medium- and high-speed corner performance but at the expense of the low-speed turns, which he described as a previous strength of the car.

And it would seem that work was successful, as Antonelli became the first driver to lap below 1m37 seconds so far this weekend. On his second set of soft tyres he set a 1m36.302s best to end the session fastest.

Red Bull continued its strong practice form in FP3, with Max Verstappen second-fastest but almost three tenths down on Antonelli.

Verstappen’s team-mate Isack Hadjar backed that up with the third-fastest time. He complained of the recently upgraded RB22 being “so unpredictable” through Turns 1 and 9 early on, before ending the session 0.558s off the pace.

George Russell was only fourth in the other Mercedes, six tenths off Antonelli, while the Ferraris of Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton rounded out the top six, seven tenths off the pace and separated by just 0.025s.

With track temperatures running in the mid-50s°C, the tyres were only good for a single flying lap and couldn’t produce better laptimes even after several cool-down laps or time in the pits.

McLaren struggled to extract performance from the soft compound in FP3 and ended up seventh and eighth, with Lando Norris setting his best lap on the medium (C3) tyre. He was eight tenths off the pace, while team-mate Oscar Piastri was a full second off Antonelli, having only found a tenth of a second going from medium to soft.

After a Friday spent solely focused on high-fuel long runs owing to a hefty grid penalty he faces for this race, Franco Colapinto led the way in the midfield for Alpine, 1.6s off the pace, ahead of Arvid Lindblad’s Racing Bulls and the Audi of Gabriel Bortoleto.

And Fernando Alonso indicated Aston Martin might be a Q2 threat at Sepang by setting the 12th-fastest time FP3, just over three tenths down on Colapinto’s Alpine and 0.018s up on Pierre Gasly’s.

items.title: Martin upsets Marquez to score surprise Motegi pole
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
MotoGP championship leader Jorge Martin sniped Motegi pole position from title rival Marc Marquez after a substantial turnaround from Friday practice.

Martin, who was only eighth-fastest on Friday, maximised the final sector on his second Q2 run to jump ahead of Marquez by a tenth, securing the new Motegi pole record in the process.

Marquez had held provisional Japanese Grand Prix pole after the opening runs, but couldn't improve on his second Q2 outing - which included a trip into the gravel at Turn 3.

Third title contender Marco Bezzecchi took a front-row spot for the briefest of moments in the end, before surrendering it right away to Pedro Acosta, who had used Bezzecchi as reference.

Alex Marquez (Gresini Ducati) completed a top five covered by just 0.175s, ahead of Fabio Di Giannantonio (VR46 Ducati), Enea Bastianini (Tech3 KTM), and Q1 graduate Raul Fernandez (Trackhouse Aprilia).

LCR team-mates Diogo Moreira and Johann Zarco were next up, Zarco crashing in Q2, while Ai Ogura - who, like team-mate Fernandez, advanced from Q1 - and Fabio Quartararo rounded out the Q2 order.

Yellow flags triggered by a fast Brad Binder crash entering the Turns 12-13-14 sequence nearly compromised Fernandez in Q1 and nearly put defending Motegi winner Pecco Bagnaia through into Q2 instead - but Fernandez had enough time to go again and consign Bagnaia to fifth row on the grid.

Joining him on that row will be Ducati stablemate Franco Morbidelli and Q1 standout Somkiat Chantra. Chantra, riding as Joan Mir's substitute rider at the factory Honda team, produced a better qualifying result than any of his efforts in his full-time season in 2025 - and outqualified team-mate Luca Marini in the process.

It was a disappointing run to 18th on the grid for Fermin Aldeguer, as he outqualified only the returning Maverick Vinales and three Yamahas.
